<section id="monitoring" class="panel" hidden aria-label="Monitoring science">
<div class="section-head"><div><div class="eyebrow">Monitoring → population state</div><h2>Missing is not zero.</h2><p>An observed zero records monitoring with no nests. A missing observation records a gap in knowledge. Those carry different biological information.</p></div><span class="tag">Methods §2.2–2.3, §3.1</span></div>
<div class="science-columns"><div><h3>What happens to inference?</h3><div class="control-stack"><button data-stress="months" aria-pressed="true">What if I lose monthly observations?</button><button data-stress="years" aria-pressed="false">What if I only monitor every few years?</button><button data-stress="short" aria-pressed="false">What if my time series is short?</button></div><div class="callout" id="stress-message" aria-live="polite"></div><details><summary>What did the experiment actually test?</summary><p>Controlled synthetic monitoring, 1996–2025. Random removal of 10–90% of months; monitoring every 2–10 years; or terminal years shortened from 2022 to 2000. Each retained record passes through Fourier reconstruction, annual aggregation, clutch-frequency conversion, and the state-space fit.</p><p>Short histories here mean <strong>retrospective terminal truncation</strong>. Data after the new endpoint are excluded, not imputed. Population-state recovery is evaluated against truth at that endpoint.</p></details></div><div class="surface"><div class="eyebrow">Observation pattern · schematic</div><div id="monitor-pattern"></div><div class="legend"><span>■ monitored</span><span>▧ unmonitored</span></div><div class="mini-title" id="stress-title"></div><svg id="stress-chart" class="chart" viewBox="0 0 600 205" role="img" aria-label="Schematic uncertainty in reconstructed nests or population trend"></svg><p class="chart-caption" id="stress-caption"></p></div></div>
<div class="deep"><details><summary>How do monthly observations become annual nesters?</summary><p>Reconstruct latent monthly abundance using the retained Bayesian Fourier model, transform posterior latent counts back from log scale, then sum within the defined nesting season. Annual nest counts enter at aggregation; annual-nester inputs enter after clutch-frequency conversion.</p><div class="equation">N<sub>obs,j,k</sub> = Nests<sub>j,k</sub> / CF <small>Eq. 3</small></div><p>For example, 550 nests ÷ 5.5 clutches per female = 100 annual nesters. CF is fixed in the baseline. This does not estimate males, immature turtles, or all adult females.</p><details><summary>Show the Fourier relationship</summary><div class="equation">s<sub>t,m</sub> = β₁ cos(2πm / ω) + β₂ sin(2πm / ω)</div><p>The seasonal increment enters a latent log-count process with dependence on the preceding month; observations have a separate error term. Periodicity is specified for nesting phenology (e.g., 12 or 6 months). The calendar follows the defined nesting season, including seasons crossing calendar years.</p></details></details>
<details><summary>What does the shared-trend state-space model estimate?</summary><div class="equation">T<sub>j</sub> = T<sub>j−1</sub> + r + ω<sub>j</sub>, &nbsp; ω<sub>j</sub> ∼ N(0,Q) <small>Eq. 4</small></div><div class="equation">log N<sub>obs,j,k</sub> = T<sub>j</sub> + a<sub>k</sub> + v<sub>j,k</sub>, &nbsp; v<sub>j,k</sub> ∼ N(0,R<sub>k</sub>) <small>Eq. 5</small></div><details><summary>What is T?</summary><p>T is the latent log annual-nester state on the reference-site scale. In the R code it is named X. It is not a nest count and is not Take; Take is written ANEᵀ in the paper.</p></details><details><summary>What is Q?</summary><p>Q is process variance: year-to-year departures from the shared log-scale population trend. Its standard deviation is √Q. Trend r is called U in the R code.</p></details><details><summary>What is observation variance?</summary><p>Rₖ describes residual variation of site k’s log observations around its latent population signal. It is distinct from Q. Annual-nester point inputs remain noisy observations, not exact latent states.</p></details><details><summary>Why are there site offsets?</summary><p>Sites have different abundance levels but share a trend. Constant aₖ scales each site relative to the reference (a₁ = 0). This assumes a shared trend and stable relative site scaling; it does not infer an independent trend for every beach.</p></details></details>
<details><summary>What exactly starts the projection?</summary><div class="equation">N<sub>final</sub> = ∑<sub>k</sub> exp(T<sub>final</sub> + a<sub>k</sub>), &nbsp; a₁ = 0 <small>Eq. 6</small></div><p>For each retained posterior row, sum across modeled sites in the final year. That annual-nester draw (N_fym0 in the app) is paired with U and Q from the same row. A single site reduces to exp(T_final).</p><p>The separate adult-female reporting quantity is RI/4 × the sum of the final four annual-nester states. It never replaces the projection initializer.</p></details>
<details><summary>What assumptions and uncertainty need attention?</summary><p>The retained Gaussian log-count model requires positive observed counts. Observed zeroes must not be silently recoded as missing or offset by an arbitrary constant. The app flags incompatible zero input; the observation model or preprocessing decision requires explicit scientific justification.</p><p>Imputation posterior draws are retained for inspection, but the app passes summarized annual estimates into the trend fit. It does not fit a single joint monthly-to-projection posterior. See the uncertainty map for this boundary.</p></details><details><summary>Show methods lineage and developer diagnostics</summary><p>Retains Eguchi Fourier imputation and Martin shared-trend annual-nester model lineage. The Shiny Developer view exposes retained chains, trace and posterior plots, R-hat, effective sample sizes, and Geweke screening. MARSS supplies an additional diagnostic, not a replacement projection posterior.</p><a href="guide/developer.html#monitoring-code">Inspect the implementation map →</a></details></div>
</section>
<section id="impact" class="panel" hidden aria-label="Take and first nesting">
<div class="section-head"><div><div class="eyebrow">Impact → expected annual-nester contribution</div><h2>Same turtle count. Different consequence.</h2><p>Move starting size. One certain-fatal interaction can remove a small, delayed contribution—or a much larger contribution in the first modeled year.</p></div><span class="tag">Methods demonstration · D = 1</span></div>
<div class="science-columns"><div><label for="size">Starting straight carapace length <output id="size-value" for="size"></output></label><input id="size" type="range" min="10" max="99" step="0.5" value="50"><div class="presets" aria-label="Paper starting sizes"><button data-size="25">25% L∞</button><button data-size="50">50% L∞</button><button data-size="75">75% L∞</button><button data-size="97.5">97.5% L∞</button><button data-size="99">99% L∞</button></div><div class="callout">Raw-count accounting would assign <strong>1 annual nester</strong>to every turtle. ANE retains survival, timing, sex, and nesting participation.</div><details><summary>Show demonstration parameters</summary><p>Leatherback composite from the Methods script; not a regional assessment. L∞ = 142.7 cm SCL; k = 0.2262 yr⁻¹; t₀ = −0.17 yr; L_mat = 139.1325 cm; logistic scale = 6.3399 cm; juvenile survival = 0.81; adult survival = 0.893; p(F) = 0.73; RI = 3.06 yr. Fixed inputs, 60-year horizon, one affected turtle, D = 1.</p></details></div><div class="surface"><div class="eyebrow">Expected loss schedule · annual-nester units</div><svg id="ane-chart" class="chart" viewBox="0 0 600 250" role="img" aria-label="Annual ANE loss by year since interaction"></svg><div class="legend"><span><i class="coral"></i>selected size</span><span><i></i>99% L∞ reference</span></div><div class="metric-row" aria-live="polite"><div class="metric"><strong id="survival-value"></strong><span>survive to first nesting¹</span></div><div class="metric"><strong id="timing-value"></strong><span>years to 50% of ANE</span></div><div class="metric"><strong id="total-value"></strong><span>cumulative ANE</span></div></div><svg id="cumulative-chart" class="chart" viewBox="0 0 600 150" role="img" aria-label="Cumulative ANE over 60 modeled years"></svg><p class="chart-caption">¹ Σ Sⱼ p(FNⱼ), over 60 years, before sex and RI. Both schedules use a common vertical scale. Year 1 is the first modeled transition.</p></div></div>
<div class="deep"><details><summary>When is this turtle expected to first enter the annual nesting population?</summary><p>A turtle can enter the first-nesting distribution only once. Being capable of nesting in year j is different from nesting for the first time in year j.</p><div class="equation">p(FN<sub>i,j</sub>) = p(T<sub>i,j</sub>) ∏<sub>h&lt;j</sub>[1 − p(T<sub>i,h</sub>)] <small>Eq. 9</small></div><p>Multiply the transition probability this year by the probability of no previous transition.</p><div class="surface"><strong>A three-year example</strong><p>If transition probabilities are 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, first-nesting probabilities are 0.2, 0.4, 0.4. They sum to 1—not 1.7.</p><div class="prob-bar" style="display:flex;height:30px;color:white;font-size:14px;text-align:center"><span style="width:20%;background:#287e78">0.2</span><span style="width:40%;background:#47734a">0.4</span><span style="width:40%;background:#8c6a25">0.4</span></div></div><details><summary>Show the growth relationship</summary><div class="equation">L(A) = L∞[1 − exp{−k(A − t₀)}] <small>Eq. 7</small></div><p>Starting age is obtained by the inverse von Bertalanffy relationship. The first-nesting transition is logistic in length: p(T) = 1/[1 + exp{−(L − L_mat)/σ_mat}], forced to 1 at 99% L∞ in the baseline (Eq. 8).</p><p>The code retains its specific forced-age sequence. First-nesting transition is a demographic proxy; it is not a direct observation of physiological maturity.</p></details><details><summary>Show survival weighting</summary><div class="equation">ϕ<sub>i,j</sub> = [1 − p(T<sub>i,j</sub>)]ϕ<sub>juv</sub> + p(T<sub>i,j</sub>)ϕ<sub>adult</sub><br>S<sub>i,j</sub> = ∏<sub>h=1…j</sub> ϕ<sub>i,h</sub> <small>Eqs. 10–11</small></div><p>The continuous transition probability weights juvenile and adult survival before first-event allocation. Survival through the first interval is included.</p></details><details><summary>Why expected value rather than Bernoulli?</summary><p>The analytical first-event probability replaces a realized yes/no first-nesting history. It preserves the expected first-nesting-only contribution in aggregate-count workflows while avoiding extra Bernoulli noise. Sex and interaction mortality are also probability weights, not additional yes/no draws.</p></details><details><summary>Show validation and methods lineage</summary><p>For every size, Σp(FN) ≤ 1. At the forced threshold, all first-event mass occurs in the first modeled year. This is an expected-value extension of the Siders first-nesting-only method; it does not claim line-for-line reproduction of every historical stochastic codebase.</p><a href="guide/developer.html#validation">Inspect mathematical checks →</a></details></details>
<details><summary>How is Take calculated? Show each term.</summary><div class="equation">ANE<sup>T</sup><sub>i,j</sub> = S<sub>i,j</sub> p(FN<sub>i,j</sub>) p(F) (1/RI) D<sub>i</sub> <small>Eq. 12</small></div><dl class="terms"><dt>S</dt><dd>Survives from interaction through that future interval.</dd><dt>p(FN)</dt><dd>First enters the nesting distribution in that year.</dd><dt>p(F)</dt><dd>Probability female.</dd><dt>1/RI</dt><dd>Annual nesting participation.</dd><dt>D</dt><dd>Mortality probability caused by the interaction.</dd></dl><p>Sum over affected individuals and cohorts (Eq. 13), retaining calendar-year alignment. Already at the threshold, one affected adult contributes ϕ_adult p(F) D / RI in the first modeled year (Eq. 14).</p><p>Take is a <strong>schedule of expected annual-nester contribution lost</strong>. It is neither all charged in the interaction year nor repeatedly counted as new first nesting in later years. Cumulative ANE is a sum of this allocation, not lifetime reproductive output.</p></details><details><summary>What data and assumptions are required?</summary><p>Affected turtles by year, size or biological stage, growth parameters, survival, first-nesting relationship, probability female, RI, and interaction mortality. Threat counts are animals affected, not deaths already multiplied by mortality. A median size alone represents a cohort; optional size-distribution inputs change that assumption.</p><p>The baseline fixes biological inputs. The app additionally supports selected uncertainty inputs; this size demonstration isolates the fixed-parameter translation.</p></details></div>
</section>
<section id="give" class="panel" hidden aria-label="Counterfactual conservation Give">
<div class="section-head"><div><div class="eyebrow">Conservation → incremental cohort → Give ANE</div><h2>What did the intervention actually add?</h2><p>Give begins with the individuals that would not otherwise have survived or been produced. The counterfactual comes first.</p></div><span class="tag">Methods extension · Eqs. 15–18</span></div>
<div class="pills" aria-label="Conservation examples"><button data-give="nest" aria-pressed="true">Nest protection</button><button data-give="release" aria-pressed="false">Headstarting / release</button><button data-give="adult" aria-pressed="false">Adult protection</button></div>
<div class="science-columns" style="margin-top:22px"><div><div id="give-fields"></div><div id="give-accounting" class="callout" aria-live="polite"></div><p class="fine">Worked examples, not fitted intervention effects. Inputs are fixed here.</p><div class="equation">Δn<sub>a</sub> = E(n<sub>a</sub> | I=1) − E(n<sub>a</sub> | I=0) <small>Eq. 15</small></div></div><div class="surface"><h3 id="give-entry"></h3><div id="give-route" class="translation"></div><svg id="give-chart" class="chart" viewBox="0 0 600 250" role="img" aria-label="Expected annual Give ANE schedule"></svg><div class="metric-row"><div class="metric"><strong id="give-extra"></strong><span>incremental individuals</span></div><div class="metric"><strong id="give-total"></strong><span>cumulative Give ANE</span></div><div class="metric"><strong id="give-time"></strong><span>years to 50% of ANE</span></div></div><p class="chart-caption">The first modeled year is the census after the intervention’s first survival interval. Plot scale is fixed across these three default examples; it expands for larger entered amounts.</p></div></div>
<div class="deep"><details><summary>Show the demographic translation</summary><div class="equation">ANE<sup>G</sup><sub>a,j</sub> = Δn<sub>a</sub> S<sub>a,j</sub> p(FN<sub>a,j</sub>) p(F) (1/RI) <small>Eq. 16</small></div><p>Same demographic ingredients; intervention-specific entry point. The conservation kernel evaluates survival over the interval and first nesting at its destination census. Newly emerged hatchlings receive a separate first-year survival probability (0.0625 in the paper demonstration), then juvenile/adult survival. Release age matters.</p></details><details><summary>How does nest protection define additional hatchlings?</summary><div class="equation">ΔH = N<sub>nest</sub> E (p<sub>emerge,I</sub> − p<sub>emerge,0</sub>) <small>Eq. 18</small></div><p>The paper example is 1 nest × 77.9 eggs × (0.70 − 0.60) = 7.79 additional emerged hatchlings. These are <strong>not 7.79 annual nesters</strong>. Emergence here is per egg and already includes hatching and emergence success; do not multiply hatching success twice.</p></details><details><summary>Why is adult protection different?</summary><div class="equation">ANE<sup>G</sup><sub>adult</sub> = ϕ<sub>adult</sub> p(F) / RI <small>Eq. 17</small></div><p>One adult death genuinely prevented enters at the adult threshold. It contributes at the next modeled annual census after adult survival. With identical parameters and D=1, it matches the magnitude of adult Take; their positions in the population transition remain different.</p></details><details><summary>What assumptions and validation matter?</summary><p>The counterfactual must concern the same cohort, period, and biological entry point. Total releases are not automatically additional animals. Do not credit the same avoided death both as reduced Take and as Give in the same scenario.</p><p>No improvement above the counterfactual must yield zero Give. A negative increment is an adverse effect, not a positive Give; the teaching form flags it rather than granting credit. Counterfactual uncertainty is not automatically estimated by the fixed-parameter baseline.</p><a href="guide/developer.html#validation">Show implementation checks →</a></details></div>
</section>
<section id="projection" class="panel" hidden aria-label="Matched population projections">
<div class="section-head"><div><div class="eyebrow">Population state + impact schedules → comparison</div><h2>Change the action. Share the future.</h2><p>Each comparison receives the same starting draw, paired U/Q values, and stochastic realization z. Differences then come from Take and Give.</p></div><span class="tag">Teaching simulation · synthetic draws</span></div>
<div class="steps"><div class="step"><span>01 · current annual nesters</span><strong>Nₜ − Takeₜ</strong></div><div class="step"><span>02 · background trend</span><strong>× exp(Uₜ)</strong></div><div class="step"><span>03 · process variation</span><strong>+ √Qₜ zₜ</strong></div><div class="step"><span>04 · translated benefit</span><strong>+ Giveₜ</strong></div><div class="step"><span>05 · safeguard</span><strong>max(0, Nₜ₊₁)</strong></div></div>
<div class="science-columns"><div><h3>One shared future ledger</h3><p class="fine">One illustrative trajectory shown from 160 synthetic draws. U and Q stay paired; year 1 uses the starting row.</p><table class="ledger"><thead><tr><th>Year</th><th>Row</th><th>U</th><th>Q</th><th>z</th></tr></thead><tbody id="future-ledger"></tbody></table><div class="scenario-branches"><span>Status quo</span><span class="take">Take</span><span class="give">Give</span><span>Take + Give</span></div><button id="resample" class="button">Draw another shared future</button><div class="fields" style="margin-top:18px"><label>Annual Take ANE<input id="take-amount" type="number" min="0" max="50" step="1" value="3"></label><label>Annual Give ANE<input id="gain-amount" type="number" min="0" max="50" step="1" value="2"></label></div><p class="fine">These are already-translated, illustrative annual schedules. Set both to zero to see exact overlap.</p><p id="projection-message" class="fine" aria-live="polite"></p></div><div class="surface"><svg id="projection-chart" class="chart" viewBox="0 0 600 260" role="img" aria-label="Matched annual-nester trajectories with uncertainty ribbon"></svg><div class="legend"><span><i></i>Status quo</span><span><i class="coral"></i>Take</span><span><i class="green"></i>Give</span><span><i style="background:#ac812d"></i>Take + Give</span></div><div class="mini-title">Paired differences from status quo</div><svg id="difference-chart" class="chart" viewBox="0 0 600 190" role="img" aria-label="Scenario minus status quo for matched draws"></svg><p class="chart-caption">Lines: medians across matched synthetic trajectories. Upper ribbon: status-quo 90% interval. Lower ribbons: 90% intervals of within-draw differences. These are not fitted population results.</p></div></div>
<div class="deep"><details><summary>Show the exact annual transition</summary><div class="equation">N<sub>t+1</sub> = max[0, max(0,N<sub>t</sub> − Take<sub>t</sub>) exp(U<sub>t</sub>) + √Q<sub>t</sub> z<sub>t</sub> + Give<sub>t</sub>]<small>Eqs. 19–22</small></div><p>The inner safeguard prevents Take from producing negative remaining abundance. The outer safeguard prevents negative census abundance after noise and Give. The paper uses r for the trend; the app calls it U.</p></details><details><summary>Why does Take precede growth, while Give follows it?</summary><p>Take removes expected annual-nester contribution before background growth, retaining the historical ordering. Give has already been propagated from its biological entry point to the destination annual census. It is added after the background transition so it does not receive that growth step again.</p><p>This is an accounting convention, not a claim that all mortality physically happens before all conservation in a calendar year. App schedule year labels refer to the destination census: 2027 labels the 2026 → 2027 transition.</p></details><details><summary>How are posterior rows matched?</summary><p>The initializer uses final annual nesters, U, and Q from one joint posterior row. The first transition uses that row. For later transitions, the retained dynamic mode samples rows without replacement within a trajectory’s later-year sequence, preserving U/Q pairing. The same row-index matrix and standard-normal z matrix feed all scenarios.</p><p>Dynamic sampling of fitted U/Q rows is already implemented. Time-varying biological input schedules are a separate planned extension.</p></details><details><summary>Why is √Q added on the abundance scale?</summary><p>This is the retained historical projection convention: Q is estimated as log-model process variance, while √Q z is added on the abundance scale in projection. The site preserves and exposes that convention; it is not quietly replaced with multiplicative lognormal noise.</p></details><details><summary>Show validation</summary><p>Zero Take and Give reproduce status quo exactly for every matched draw. Row pairing and shared future noise are checked separately. Adult Take/Give symmetry tests demographic translation, not cancellation after the asymmetrically ordered growth step.</p><a href="guide/developer.html#validation">See what each check establishes →</a></details></div>
</section>
<section id="uncertainty" class="panel" hidden aria-label="Uncertainty and planned extensions">
<div class="section-head"><div><div class="eyebrow">Know what the model knows</div><h2>The currency is shared. Uncertainty remains.</h2><p>Distinguish retained posterior uncertainty, fixed assumptions, optional app inputs, and future work.</p></div></div>
<div class="uncertainty-list">
<details open><summary>Monitoring gaps <span class="status-label">posterior retained</span></summary><p>Fourier latent states and parameters are sampled. Annual estimates passed downstream are summarized; imputation uncertainty is not fully coupled to the annual state-space posterior.</p></details>
<details open><summary>Observation and population state <span class="status-label">posterior retained</span></summary><p>Rₖ, latent annual-nester states, shared trend U, and process variance Q are estimated. Joint row association is retained for projection initialization.</p></details>
<details><summary>Future process <span class="status-label">stochastic</span></summary><p>Future standard-normal z realizes process noise. U/Q rows are dynamically sampled as paired values. Scenarios share both, so a management comparison is not confounded by different random futures.</p></details>
<details><summary>Demography <span class="status-label fixed">baseline fixed</span></summary><p>Growth, juvenile/adult survival, probability female, RI, clutch frequency, and first-nesting parameters are fixed in the Methods demonstration. The app has selected optional uncertainty controls, including growth-parameter, survival, probability-female, and RI inputs; these are not a full joint demographic posterior.</p></details>
<details><summary>Threat counts, size, mortality <span class="status-label">optional app uncertainty</span></summary><p>Selected count, log-length, and mortality uncertainty can be supplied. With zero SDs and fixed counts, the app returns the expected-value baseline. First nesting and mortality probabilities are not independently re-realized as Bernoulli outcomes.</p></details>
<details><summary>Conservation counterfactual <span class="status-label fixed">user supplied</span></summary><p>Incremental benefit and early-life survival must be justified. The fixed baseline does not estimate the causal effect of the intervention or automatically propagate its counterfactual uncertainty.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="callout"><strong>Implementation validation ≠ biological appropriateness.</strong>Correct arithmetic cannot make a borrowed survival estimate, unsupported counterfactual, or unsuitable observation model appropriate for your population.</div>
<details><summary>Planned: demographic inputs that change through time</summary><p>Future options: fixed estimate, annual values, uploaded time series, linear change, exponential change, logistic change, step change, or a covariate relationship.</p><div class="equation">logit(ϕ<sub>t</sub>) = α + β C<sub>t</sub></div><p>Cₜ might be a climate variable. This is planned functionality, not an active fitting control. The current fixed-parameter model remains the validated baseline.</p><p><strong>Regression rule:</strong> a constant dynamic schedule must reproduce the existing model exactly. Nonconstant schedules need new timing, uncertainty, and biological validation.</p></details><details><summary>What can developer diagnostics tell me?</summary><p>Inspect chain mixing, R-hat, effective sample sizes, Geweke statistics, imputation fits, and model records in Shiny. Screening thresholds do not prove convergence or biological validity. Exact replay seeds are not yet retained in the supplied app; exported chains still support inspection.</p><a href="guide/developer.html">Open technical documentation →</a></details>
</section>
